stem: An adult with severe hypertriglyceridemia is prescribed icosapent ethyl. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.A: This is a prescription EPA formulation with a defined dose and indication; nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not considered equivalent substitutes and may have variable fatty-acid content.
options.B: Any over-the-counter fish-oil capsule can be substituted dose-for-dose because all omega-3 products have standardized EPA content and identical evidence.
options.C: The medication is prescribed mainly to lower blood pressure and has little expected effect on triglycerides.
options.D: Icosapent ethyl is an EPA-plus-DHA product, so a rise in LDL-C from its DHA component is required for the medication to work.

rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling identifies icosapent ethyl as a prescription ethyl ester of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) indicated, among other labeled uses, as an adjunct to diet to reduce triglycerides in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline explicitly states that nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to prescription omega-3 medications and have variable fatty-acid content. B therefore makes an unsafe equivalence. C misstates the treatment purpose in this scenario. D is incorrect because icosapent ethyl contains EPA rather than an EPA/DHA combination.
educational_objective: Distinguish prescription icosapent ethyl from nonprescription fish-oil supplements: it is a standardized EPA medication with defined dosing and evidence, and OTC products should not be substituted as if they were dose-for-dose equivalents.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed; American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and partner societies
source_document_title: Icosapent Ethyl Capsules Prescribing Information; 2026 ACC/AHA Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
source_version_date: Icosapent ethyl label updated July 9, 2026; 2026 dyslipidemia guideline published March 13, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Icosapent ethyl label, Indications and Usage: ethyl ester of EPA indicated as adjunct to diet to reduce TG in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥500 mg/dL); Dosage and Administration: 4 g/day in divided doses with food. 2026 dyslipidemia guideline, Triglyceride-Lowering Medications: icosapent ethyl contains EPA only; nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to or considered prescription medications and have variable fatty-acid content.
source_claim_supported: Icosapent ethyl is a standardized prescription EPA product used to lower triglycerides; current guideline guidance distinguishes prescription omega-3 medications from variable-content nonprescription fish-oil supplements.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: provide medication education, distinguish prescribed therapies from non-equivalent products, and evaluate therapeutic response.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — prescription icosapent ethyl versus OTC fish oil
correction_summary: Narrowed the raw class-level statement to icosapent ethyl and replaced the vague claim about 'unregulated supplements' with the exact 2026 guideline distinction: nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent prescription medications and have variable fatty-acid content. The final item also avoids conflating EPA-only icosapent with EPA/DHA products.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against a July 2026 icosapent ethyl FDA label and the March 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A matches the prescription-product and non-equivalence guidance. B falsely treats variable OTC supplements as dose-equivalent. C misstates the indication. D falsely adds DHA to an EPA-only drug.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; prescription EPA formulation with non-equivalent OTC supplements.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; OTC products vary and are not prescription-equivalent.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; triglyceride reduction is a labeled purpose.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Naming icosapent ethyl avoids conflating different prescription omega-3 formulations and their LDL effects.
audit_findings.cueing: All options compare formulation, purpose, or composition.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication-product education fits Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked EPA-only composition, current labeled severe-TG indication, prescription-versus-OTC wording, and the distinction from EPA/DHA products. No second defensible answer remained.
